author: SW Iowa Times
title: Botna Bend Park to host National Bison Day celebration on November 7
text:
Botna Bend Park to host National Bison Day celebration on November 7
Botna Bend Park will celebrate National Bison Day on November 7 with educational activities and family events. The program highlights bison conservation and the species’ history in Iowa. Visitors can enjoy live demonstrations, music, and learn about the role of bison in prairie ecosystems.
Pottawattamie Conservation Foundation will host a National Bison Day event at Botna Bend Park on November 7, offering visitors an opportunity to learn about bison and conservation efforts. The event will take place from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. and is free with a $3 per-vehicle park entry or annual membership.
The open house-style event will feature a range of family-friendly activities, including viewing Botna Bend’s live bison herd, atlatl throwing, bison wool spinning, flint knapping, hay rack rides, bison artifacts, food by The Feed Trough, children’s crafts, fossils, and live music by Ron Cisar. The Union Pacific Railroad Museum will provide information on the history of bison and the railroad, while The Nature Conservancy will discuss the relationship between bison and the prairie. Video presentations on bison archaeological sites will also be available.
According to the Pottawattamie Conservation Foundation, "How different the world could have been without the near-extinction of the American Bison. Fueled by westward railroad expansion and other factors such as government encouragement, European settlers, big-game hunting tourism, cheap meat and hides, and a way of controlling Native American tribes, bison were decimated from an estimated 30 to 60 million to fewer than 1,000 by the late 1800s. Thanks to conservation efforts, the Plains bison population in North America has rebounded, with more than 20,000 bison currently living in conservation herds like the one at Botna Bend Park. Approximately 25,000 to 30,000 bison live on Native American reservations and tribal lands across the United States, and an estimated 400,000 bison live in commercial herds."
The last wild bison in Iowa were seen in 1870. The foundation said bison numbers have recovered significantly due to conservation efforts, though most modern bison have some domestic cattle ancestry. Bison can weigh up to 2,000 pounds, stand six feet tall at the shoulder, and run up to 45 miles per hour.
Botna Bend Park is one of several Pottawattamie Conservation parks, including Arrowhead Park, Hitchcock Nature Center, Crescent Hill at Hitchcock, Narrows River Park, and Olde Town Park. More information about the event and the parks can be found at the Pottawattamie Conservation website.
